38 In the circuit shown, a potentiometer of total resistance 120  is connected in parallel with a
resistor of resistance 150  and a resistor of resistance R.
The battery has electromotive force (e.m.f.) 12 V and negligible internal resistance.
150 Ω
120 Ω
12 V
V
R
The voltmeter reads 0 V when the slider of the potentiometer is 1
4 of the way from its lower end,
as shown.
What is resistance R ?
A
30 
B
38 
C
50 
D
450 

hints: Notice the voltmeter joins the potentiometer slider to the junction of the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor and $R$, so $0 \, \text{V}$ means those two points are at the same potential above the common lower wire.
Connect the slider position to the $120 \, \Omega$ potentiometer as a potential divider: $1/4$ from the lower end means $30 \, \Omega$ below the slider and $90 \, \Omega$ above it.
Set the potential of the $150 \, \Omega$ and $R$ divider equal to the slider potential and solve $12 \times R/(150+R)$ for $R$.
walkthrough: The $12 \, \text{V}$ battery is connected directly across the $120 \, \Omega$ potentiometer and also across the series pair $150 \, \Omega$ plus $R$, so both branches have $12 \, \text{V}$ across them.
The slider is $1/4$ of the way from the lower end, so the resistance between slider and the $0 \, \text{V}$ lower wire is $(1/4) \times 120 = 30 \, \Omega$.
By the potential divider rule, the slider potential above the lower wire is $V_s = 12 \times 30/120 = 3.0 \, \text{V}$.
Let the junction of $150 \, \Omega$ and $R$ be $V_J$ above the lower wire. For that series divider, $V_J = 12 \times R/(150+R)$.
Zero voltmeter reading means no p.d. between the points, so $V_J = V_s$. Hence $12 \times R/(150+R) = 3.0$.
Rearrange: $R/(150+R) = 1/4$, so $4R = 150 + R$ and $3R = 150$, giving $R = 50 \, \Omega$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Gives $30 \, \Omega$ by using only the $30 \, \Omega$ lower section of the potentiometer, not the ratio $R/(150+R)$ for the $150 \, \Omega$ and $R$ divider.

B.explanation: Gives about $38 \, \Omega$ from an incorrect fraction of the $12 \, \text{V}$ across $R$, not the $3 \, \text{V}$ balance condition.

D.explanation: Gives $450 \, \Omega$ by using $3/4$ of the potentiometer voltage for the lower part instead of $1/4$ from the lower end.
